# Chapter 6 — The Single Reconciled Cross-Boundary Plane

::: {.callout-note}
## In this chapter
The fifth and most defensible differentiator is the one the other four do not imply and the one Microsoft specifically cannot compose: a single organizational substrate reconciled across federal cloud boundaries. This chapter explains why Commercial, GCC-Moderate, GCC-High, and DoD are genuine boundaries rather than regions, how OrgPath spans them with boundary-aware transports and per-boundary trust anchoring, and why "one reconciled plane" is a claim no single-boundary product can make. The normative contracts are `ADR-007`, `ADR-038`, and `ADR-033`; the device-plane specification is [Where Data Lives — Devices and Azure](/customer-documents/reference-architecture/where-data-lives-devices-and-azure.html).
:::

## Boundaries Are Not Regions

In a commercial estate, "multi-cloud" usually means several regions or several providers that nonetheless talk to one another freely. Federal estates are different in a way that matters enormously here. Commercial, GCC-Moderate, GCC-High, and DoD are not regions of one cloud; they are separate clouds with separate identity authorities, separate service catalogs, separate compliance regimes, and deliberate boundaries between them. A token issued in one is not trusted in another. A service available in one may not exist in another. They are isolated by design, because the isolation is the security control.

This is the setting in which an organizational substrate has to prove itself, and it is where the convergent IGA platforms and Microsoft's primitives reveal a shared limitation. Most of them live in one boundary. A deployment is GCC-High, or it is Commercial, and the organizational structure it maintains is the structure of that one boundary. An organization that operates across boundaries — as federal programs routinely do — ends up with a separate, independently maintained copy of its org structure in each one, and no mechanism to keep them saying the same thing.

> Across federal boundaries, "keep the org structure consistent" is not a synchronization convenience. It is a problem with no native owner, because each boundary is a separate cloud that does not, by design, trust or even see the others.

## One Substrate, Boundary-Aware Transports

OrgPath's answer is to treat the boundary as a first-class property of the substrate rather than a deployment that happens once per cloud. The same fifteen-facet model, the same governed codebook, and the same drift taxonomy apply in every boundary; what changes per boundary is the transport that carries facet values to the right place and the trust root that authenticates the carrier.

The transport awareness is concrete. Identity-plane facets are written through Microsoft Graph; device-plane facets are written through Graph for Entra-joined devices and through Azure Resource Manager tags for Azure Arc-managed servers, the dual-transport doctrine ADR-038 defines. Each boundary has its own correct host for these calls and its own correct token audience, and the substrate selects them per boundary rather than assuming the Commercial defaults. A facet write destined for GCC-High goes to the GCC-High endpoint with a GCC-High-audience token; the same write for DoD goes to the DoD endpoint. The substrate is one model; the transports are boundary-correct.

> The model does not change across boundaries — the facets, the codebook, and the drift classes are identical. What changes is the host and the token audience, selected per boundary, so a write always lands in the right cloud through the right door.

## Trust Anchored Per Boundary

Spanning boundaries safely requires more than sending writes to the right endpoint; it requires being certain that the identity behind each claim is anchored to a trust root the boundary actually recognizes. This is where OrgPath adds a dedicated check that has no equivalent in the IGA platforms' organizational handling.

For each boundary, the substrate knows the declared trust anchors — the root certificate authorities whose chains it will accept. When an identity claim arrives, its certificate chain is validated against the anchor declared for that boundary: does the chain link cleanly from leaf to root, and does its terminal issuer match the anchor this boundary trusts? A chain that does not reach the declared anchor, or an adapter that claims to be certificate-anchored but declares no anchor to check against, produces an identity-drift finding of its own. The cross-boundary plane is therefore not only writing to the right cloud; it is continuously checking that every identity it acts on is rooted in that cloud's own trust, and flagging the cases where it is not.

This matters because the boundaries' isolation is exactly what an attacker or a misconfiguration would try to blur — a claim that should belong to one boundary surfacing in another. Anchoring trust per boundary, and emitting a typed finding when the anchoring fails, is how the substrate keeps the boundaries' separation intact while still reconciling structure across them.

> Reconciling across boundaries does not mean dissolving them. Each boundary keeps its own trust root; the substrate validates every claim against the right one and raises a typed finding when a chain does not anchor where it should.

## Why "One Plane" Is the Claim Microsoft Cannot Make

The earlier chapters were careful to grant Microsoft its strengths, including genuine cross-boundary capabilities — federal clouds are real Microsoft products, and there is real machinery for operating in each. The precise claim here is narrower and survives that fairness: Microsoft's own primitives cannot be composed into a *single reconciled organizational plane* across these boundaries, because the primitives that would have to compose into it do not validate, do not type their divergences, and do not nest, as the previous chapters established. Even granting full cross-boundary reach, what would be reconciled across the boundaries is unvalidated, untyped, flat organizational state — which is to say, not a substrate.

OrgPath makes the "one plane" claim because the thing being reconciled across boundaries is the substrate the first four chapters built: decomposed into facets, validated by a governed codebook, composable into a hierarchy, and self-reconciling through a typed drift engine. Spanning that substrate across boundaries with boundary-aware transports and per-boundary trust anchoring yields one organizational truth that holds in Commercial, GCC-Moderate, GCC-High, and DoD simultaneously, reconciled by one engine, expressed in one model. No single-boundary product can make that claim, and no composition of unvalidated primitives can either.

> The differentiator, in full: a deterministic, per-facet, codebook-validated organizational substrate, with a typed drift taxonomy, reconciled across federal cloud boundaries as one plane. Every clause in that sentence is a capability the previous chapters earned. The last clause is the one no surveyed platform — Microsoft included — can compose.

The five capabilities are now on the table. The final chapter assembles them into the capability matrix that shows who owns what, and lays out the sequence for filling the gap in a way that consumes an organization's existing platforms rather than replacing them.
